claims.text: High-entropy alloys possess intrinsic lattice distortion.
Intrinsic lattice distortion provides a baseline obstacle to dislocation motion.
The combination of intrinsic lattice distortion and dynamically developed local chemical order governs hardness and strength in HEAs.
The proposed initial material is a single-phase disordered FCC solid solution with minimal pre-existing local chemical order.
Cryogenic tensile deformation can promote dynamic development of local chemical order.
Controlled irradiation can induce dynamic formation of local chemical-order domains.
High-temperature annealing erases incipient local chemical order and suppresses its subsequent dynamic development.
The structural mediator consists of local-chemical-order domains that interact with intrinsic lattice distortion.
Interstitial-driven processes can enhance local chemical ordering in an FCC HEA.
Irradiation-defect-driven processes enhance local chemical ordering.
Local-chemical-order domains restrict expansion of plastic zones.
Increasing irradiation dose raises defect density and lattice distortion, thereby limiting plastic-zone expansion.
Dynamic local chemical order increases yield strength.
Dynamic local chemical order increases nanoindentation hardness.
An LCO-promoting treatment will produce higher yield strength and nanoindentation hardness than an LCO-suppressing baseline.
The proposed mechanism applies to FCC HEAs within deformation regimes in which dynamic LCO formation is active.
The governing mechanism may differ in heavily precipitated or multiphase HEAs.

contradictions.description: The comparison is described as differing only in LCO, but one set undergoes cryogenic deformation or irradiation while the other undergoes high-temperature annealing. These treatments can also alter defect density, residual strain, dislocation structure, recovery state, and potentially grain or phase structure, so the asserted microstructural equivalence is not ensured.

The mechanism acknowledges irradiation-induced defect hardening as a competing contribution, yet the proposed irradiated-versus-annealed comparison does not independently control defect density. A strength difference therefore cannot be assigned uniquely to LCO.
